extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, students, editors, and general readers interested in The Tatler and early-18th-century periodical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and editorial commentary about the aims, style, format, and production practices of The Tatler (early-18th-century periodical essays), including recommended tone, organisation by topical headings, and editorial treatment for modern editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General purpose / aim
rubrics_metrics.description: “The general purpose of this paper is to expose the false arts of life, to pull off the disguises of cunning, vanity, and affectation, and to recommend a general simplicity in our dress, our discourse, and our behaviour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tatler's work is explicitly moral and corrective: aim pieces at social vices and follies with the intention of improving manners and promoting simplicity. Examples in the text illustrate exposing vices (duelling, swindlers) and recommending virtues (truth, innocence, honour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication frequency, format, and pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: “The numbers were published three times a week, on the post-days, at the price of one penny. Each paper consisted of a single folio sheet, and the first four were distributed gratuitously.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical production rule: short, frequent issues in inexpensive format to reach a broad public; initial free distribution to build readership. Use concise sheet-length pieces rather than long tomes in early issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical organisation by coffee-house article headings
rubrics_metrics.description: “The subject of each article was to be indicated by the name of the coffee-house or other place from which it was supposed to come: 'All accounts of gallantry, pleasure, and entertainment shall be under the article of White's Chocolate-house; Poetry, under that of Will's Coffee-house; Learning, under the title of Grecian; Foreign and Domestic News you will have from Saint James's Coffee-house; and what else I have to offer on any other subject shall be dated from my own Apartment.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use familiar public venues as topical labels to orient readers and lend social authenticity. Map discrete topics to consistent headings so readers know where to look for certain material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of news paragraphs to attract readers
rubrics_metrics.description: “Steele probably thought that his position of Gazetteer would enable him to give the latest news, and he says that these paragraphs brought in a multitude of readers; but as the position of the Tatler became established, the need for the support of these items of news grew less, and after the first eighty numbers they are of rare occurrence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate timely news items early to build an audience, but allow the paper's established voice and essays to supplant news items as the core attraction. News can be a hook rather than the permanent focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: humour and raillery before severity
rubrics_metrics.description: “You must treat this custom with humour and raillery to get an audience, before you come to pronounce sentence upon it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer genial satire and lightness to open moral fire: use humour to engage readers and lead them toward reflection instead of alienating them with immediate severity. Example: handling duelling with wit before moral condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticise behaviours, not persons
rubrics_metrics.description: “The design was to expose not persons but things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target vices, customs, and social practices rather than naming or attacking individuals; use generalisation, allegory, or veiled examples to maintain moral weight without gratuitous personal invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of veiled or imaginary characters as framing devices
rubrics_metrics.description: “Follies and weaknesses are ridiculed in the Tatler in a genial spirit, by one who was fully alive to his own imperfections, and point is usually given to the papers by a sketch of some veiled or imaginary individual... Isaac Bickerstaff himself... Pacolet... Jenny Distaff...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame essays with recurring fictional personas (e.g., Isaac Bickerstaff) or club members to dramatize morals, provide continuity, and create affectionate satire. This device allows concrete illustration while avoiding direct personal attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance social gossip with sustained moral essays
rubrics_metrics.description: “The social articles are at least as interesting now as when they were written... the principal change... was the development of the sustained essay on morals or manners, and the less frequent indulgence in satire upon individual offenders.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine lighter, social/gossip pieces that reflect town-life (coffee-house scenes, theatre notes) with lengthier, reflective essays on morals and manners; the mix keeps readers entertained while conveying ethical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral emphasis on domestic life and respect for women
rubrics_metrics.description: “The general purpose of the whole has been to recommend truth, innocence, honour, and virtue... of what Coleridge called Steele's 'pure humanity' there is nowhere better evidence than in the Tatler... his respect for women... dwell[ing] on the happiness of marriage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevate domestic scenes and sympathetic portraits (marriage, children, private grief) to instruct and move readers; portray respect for women and private virtues as social ideals rather than merely rhetorical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate intelligent literary criticism and cultural uplift
rubrics_metrics.description: “'The vitiated tastes of the audience at the theatre could only be amended by encouraging the representation of the noble characters drawn by Shakespeare and others'... allusions to 'Paradise Lost'... comparison of passages by Milton and Dryden.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the periodical to improve public taste: defend and recommend canonical literature and noble drama; include comparative criticism and references to high models (Shakespeare, Milton) to elevate readers' aesthetic sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial practice: textual accuracy, annotation and use of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: “Scrupulous accuracy in the text has been aimed at, but the eccentricities of spelling... have not been preserved, and the punctuation has occasionally been corrected... I have endeavoured to preserve what is of value in the older editions, and to supplement it... by such further information as appeared desirable... useful illustrations have been found in the contemporary newspapers and periodicals.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For modern editions: aim for careful transcription, correct obvious printing eccentricities, provide concise annotation and references, consult earlier annotated editions and contemporary sources (diaries, newspapers) to clarify obscure passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality in praise and criticism (avoid party bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I mention this only to defend myself against the imputation of being moved rather by party than opinion; and I think it is apparent, I have with the utmost frankness allowed merit wherever I found it, though joined in interests different from those ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works and persons on merit, not partisan affiliation. Allow praise where deserved regardless of political or social alignment; avoid letting party commitments dictate editorial judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of motto/quotation to frame each number
rubrics_metrics.description: “The motto of the first forty numbers was 'Quicquid agunt homines ... nostri farrago libelli'; but in the following numbers it was changed to 'Celebrare domestica facta'; and afterwards each number generally had a quotation bearing upon the subject of the day.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an epigraph or motto relevant to the day's topic to signal theme and set a reflective tone; changing mottoe can reflect evolution of editorial purpose.
